prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. After the first round the case has been tested from several sides and has held. Seven of eight files name the same part and the same two laureates, and the eighth, Eriksson, accepts it as a good outcome and disagrees only about weight. I do not count that as evidence; what matters is that the objections raised are about framing and not about the science. The achievement is a specific idea, trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the lattice light does not shift the clock transition, together with a decisive experimental demonstration at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, reproduced independently in several national laboratories and compared routinely between them. It gives measurable consequences: tests of constancy of fundamental parameters and of relativity, relativistic geodesy, and a basis for a later redefinition of the second. The credit is two names, Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking the strontium clock to record accuracy and stability, which fits the three-person limit without an arbitrary exclusion. In answer to the chair's first question, I think the citation can be written to separate this from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems by naming the lattice mechanism and the 10^-18 outcome explicitly, and by not using the words optical clocks or frequency standards on their own.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes remains the strongest reservation, and I should not dismiss it just because I think it is answerable. A committee could still read this as the third prize in one precision-measurement tradition, and a prize for a record in accuracy is less clearly a new phenomenon than a prize for a new state of matter or a new observational window. Lemonde, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock programmes are outside the credit, and Ido and Kimble had earlier trapping ideas, so the claim that Katori and Ye are the originators and the decisive demonstrators needs to be stated carefully in the citation and not overclaimed. I am a string theorist and cosmologist and not an expert in atomic physics, and Lindroth and Kroll are right that two atomic physicists, myself not included, share a disciplinary lens; I rely on the evidence and on colleagues outside the field.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B053 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a new organising principle for a field, accepts B057 as a good outcome, and is asked by the chair what would need to change for him to move B057 ahead.
responses.response: I take the organising-principle argument seriously and I agree that fifteen years of confirmation across many materials is a real strength. My difficulty is attribution and overlap. The credit among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Hasan is not settled by choosing three names, and you yourself say the Hasan versus Mele choice would force a name out. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions also sits close to the concept. The clock has neither problem to the same degree. So I would ask whether you see a three-name B053 that you consider fair to the people left out; if you do, I would like to see the citation wording, and I would then treat B053 as the stronger alternative than B015. I do not see that the breadth of top-three support for B053 should settle it, and I would not want to use support counts in place of that argument.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from the cavity method to B057 on the merits and notes that the line against the 2005 and 2012 prizes is not as sharp as for a new phenomenon, and that Ido and Kimble had earlier trapping ideas.
responses.response: I agree that the line is less sharp than for a new phenomenon, and I accept the point about Ido and Kimble as part of the history of the concept. I would answer that proposing that a magic condition might exist is different from showing that it can be met in practice and evaluating all systematics at this level, and that second step is what Katori and Ye did. That is also why I would draft the citation around the realisation and the performance, with the invention named, so that it does not claim more than the record supports. On your own first choice, I would still not rank the cavity method above the clock given that only one member ranks it, and the separation from the 2021 prize is not yet clear to me.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the redefinition of the second is a later metrological decision and not a precondition, and discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory for the chair to judge.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition is not a precondition, and I now say so more firmly than in round one: the achievement is complete because independent clocks agree at the 10^-18 level. The citation should rest on that demonstrated capability and not on the redefinition. On your disclosure, I see a stay in a laboratory of a 2005 laureate as scientific lineage and not a connection to Katori or Ye, and I would not ask for recusal, but I leave the judgement to the chair as you suggest.

responses.point: Pearce, who opened with IceCube, now prefers B057 and keeps B054 as an alternative, noting that the larger open question may be a new observational window.
responses.response: I appreciate that you moved on the merits and I agree that B054 is a real discovery. I ranked IceCube highly at opening and I do propose Halzen, Karle and Spiering there, so I accept that the credit can be argued. My concern remains that the diffuse flux is secure while source associations are few and of moderate significance, and that the decisive contributions of these three are hard to separate from AMANDA, Baikal and the collaboration. For that reason I keep it as a later candidate and not as a rival to the clock this year, and I do not list it among my two alternatives, although I would not object if the committee found the credit argument persuasive.

responses.point: Olsson accepts B057 but says the lattice clock could be read as a refinement of precision metrology and that single-ion optical clocks are a parallel line partly absorbed by the 2012 prize.
responses.response: I share that reservation and I think it is the right test. The 2012 prize recognised control of individual trapped quantum systems; the lattice clock gets its stability by interrogating a very large number of neutral atoms at once with the perturbation of the lattice cancelled, which single ions cannot do, and that difference is why I regard it as a separate achievement. I would not claim more than that. If the committee accepts that, a pair citation to Katori and Ye does not need to acknowledge the ion-clock programmes, though the citation text should avoid language that implies they were not honoured.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice mechanism and the 10^-18 realisation separate the prize sufficiently from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
Whether Ye's role is best credited as record accuracy and stability or as the broader many-body clock programme, and how to word it without understating Takamoto, Lemonde and others.
Whether B053 should be considered stronger if a fair three-name credit can be found among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the BHZ authors, given the 2016 overlap.
Whether the redefinition of the second should have any bearing on timing; I now think it should not.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. None of the credited names on the shortlisted ballots is my PhD supervisor (Gross), early mentor (Rubinstein), frequent co-author (Van Riet) or a member of the Uppsala theoretical-physics group. I am a string theorist and cosmologist, so my closeness to the subject is only that of a theoretical physicist; I rely on the evidence in the first-round statements for the details of precision atomic physics. No change since round one.
